# v2.95-dev

A development-process release. Nothing in the application changes — this is
about how changes get into it.

Until now, a change reached the dev channel the moment it was pushed: the push
itself created the release. The checks that existed ran *alongside* that push,
so a problem was found after the release had already been published, not before.
From this release, changes arrive through pull requests, and the checks have to
pass before anything can merge.

## Changed

- **Work now lands through pull requests.** A change is developed on its own
  short-lived branch and opened as a pull request against `dev`; promoting to
  the stable channel is a second pull request from `dev` to `master`. The
  release is still created automatically by the merge, exactly as before, so
  nothing about how releases are tagged or how systems find them has changed.

- **Every pull request is built before it can merge.** The automated checks now
  run a full production build in addition to the existing code style, type and
  permission checks. The build is the step that fails during an update on a live
  server — running it here means that failure happens on a pull request instead
  of on your machine, halfway through an update.

- **The release checklist is now checked automatically.** Three rules that were
  previously followed by hand are verified on every pull request: that the
  version number has moved by exactly one step, that the lock file agrees with
  it, and that the release notes you are reading right now were actually
  written. A missed version bump used to result in a release that silently
  cut nothing; it is now caught before merging.

- **An advisory scan looks for identifying details in each change.** This
  project ships as a generic product, so example data in the code, the
  documentation and these release notes must stay fictional. A new check flags
  email addresses outside the fictional example domains and file paths that name
  a real account. It is advisory only — it reports, it never blocks — and it
  deliberately does not try to detect real company or person names.

- **A pull request template** now carries the full post-change checklist, so
  nothing depends on remembering it.

## Upgrading

Nothing to do. There are no database changes, no configuration changes, and no
change to the application itself. If you run an installation, this release is
functionally identical to v2.94.
